# Rules

<!-- Generated by `faultline rules --markdown`; do not edit by hand. -->

Every finding Faultline reports belongs to one of these rules. Severity is
not fixed per rule: it depends on whether values flow into or out of the API
at the change, and on the evidence found (see
[comparison internals](internals/comparison.md)).

## FL1001

**type-changed** — The type of a value changed

The value at this position now has a different JSON type or shape, for example a string that became an integer. Values of the old type are rejected (in requests) or unexpected (in responses).

Introduce the new type alongside the old one, for example as a union, and remove the old one in a later major version.

## FL1002

**property-added** — A property was added

An object gained a declared property. A new *required* property in a request breaks every client that does not send it. In a response, a new property is usually safe, but clients that reject unknown properties may fail.

Make new request properties optional, with a server-side default.

## FL1003

**property-removed** — A property was removed

An object no longer declares a property. Clients that read it from responses lose data; in requests, the property is now subject to `additionalProperties` and may be rejected.

Deprecate the property first and keep it until the next major version.

## FL1004

**property-requirement-changed** — A property became required or optional

A property that was optional became required, or the reverse. Making a request property required breaks clients that omit it; making a response property optional breaks clients that rely on its presence.

## FL1005

**enum-value-added** — An enum value was added

An enumeration gained a value. In requests this only widens what is accepted. In responses, clients with exhaustive handling (a `switch` without a default branch, generated enums) may fail on the new value.

## FL1006

**enum-value-removed** — An enum value was removed

An enumeration lost a value. Requests using it are rejected. In responses this is safe: the value is simply no longer produced.

## FL1007

**bound-changed** — A numeric or size constraint changed

A `minimum`, `maximum`, `multipleOf`, length, item-count or property-count constraint changed. Tightening a request constraint rejects values that used to be accepted; loosening a response constraint can produce values clients do not expect (for example strings longer than a fixed-size buffer).

## FL1008

**numeric-kind-changed** — An integer became a number or vice versa

Changing `integer` to `number` lets responses carry fractional values that clients parsing integers reject; changing `number` to `integer` rejects fractional request values.

## FL1009

**pattern-changed** — A string pattern changed

The regular expression constraining a string changed. Faultline compares patterns as regular languages and shows the shortest string one version accepts and the other rejects; patterns it cannot analyse (backreferences, lookaround) are reported as risky.

## FL1010

**format-changed** — A format annotation changed

The `format` of a value changed, for example `int32` to `int64` or `date` to `date-time`. Formats are annotations in JSON Schema, but generated code and validators often enforce them.

## FL1011

**uniqueness-changed** — Array uniqueness changed

`uniqueItems` was added or removed. Requiring unique items rejects requests with duplicates; allowing duplicates in responses can surprise clients that relied on uniqueness.

## FL1012

**variant-added** — A union alternative was added

A union (`anyOf`, `oneOf`, a nullable type) gained an alternative. Responses may now contain values clients do not handle, such as `null`. For `oneOf`, a new alternative can also make previously valid values ambiguous and therefore invalid.

## FL1013

**variant-removed** — A union alternative was removed

A union lost an alternative. Requests using that alternative are rejected.

## FL1014

**union-mode-changed** — A union changed between anyOf and oneOf

Switching between `anyOf` and `oneOf` changes whether a value may match several alternatives.

## FL1015

**composition-changed** — Composed constraints changed

Constraints expressed through composition (`allOf`, `not`, dependent requirements, pattern properties) changed in a way without a finer description. The severity follows the values Faultline could show to be lost or gained.

## FL1016

**discriminator-changed** — A discriminator property changed

The property that selects a union alternative changed, appeared or disappeared. Clients and servers that dispatch on it disagree.

## FL1017

**discriminator-value-added** — A discriminator value was added

A new discriminator value selects an alternative. Responses using it may not be handled by existing clients.

## FL1018

**discriminator-value-removed** — A discriminator value was removed

A discriminator value no longer selects an alternative. Requests using it are rejected.

## FL1019

**discriminator-value-retargeted** — A discriminator value selects a different schema

The same discriminator value now selects a different alternative, so the same payload is interpreted differently.

## FL1020

**deprecation-changed** — Deprecation status changed

An element was deprecated or un-deprecated. Not a break by itself, but a signal to plan removal.

## FL1021

**access-changed** — readOnly or writeOnly changed

A value became read-only or write-only, or stopped being so. Read-only values are ignored in requests and write-only values are never returned, so this changes which direction the value participates in.

## FL1022

**default-changed** — A default value changed

The default used when a value is omitted changed. Requests that omit the value now behave differently.

## FL1023

**schema-added** — A schema was added

A standalone schema was added.

## FL1024

**schema-removed** — A schema was removed

A standalone schema was removed; everything that used it loses its contract.

## FL1025

**field-renamed** — A field was renamed

A field kept its identity but changed its name: its number (Protobuf tag) stayed, or the new name lists the old one as an alias (Avro). Binary data still resolves, but generated code no longer compiles against the old name, and encodings that use field names without alias support stop recognising it.

Keep the old name, or add the new field alongside the old one and deprecate the old one.

## FL1026

**field-number-changed** — A field's number changed

A field kept its name but moved to another number (Protobuf tag). Binary data written with the old number is read as an unknown field or, worse, as whatever field now has that number.

Field numbers are permanent: add a new field instead, and reserve the old number when the old field is removed.

## FL1027

**field-aliases-changed** — Alternative names of a field changed

The other names a field is accepted under changed, such as a Protobuf `json_name` or an Avro alias. Data written under a removed name is no longer recognised and the value is silently dropped.

## FL1028

**field-group-changed** — A field's oneof membership changed

A field moved into or out of a `oneof`, or its `oneof` gained or lost members. Adding a field to a group means messages that set it together with another member are no longer valid: one of the two values is dropped. Removing a field from a group lets receivers see combinations they never saw before.

Only add *new* fields to an existing `oneof`.

## FL1029

**enum-value-renumbered** — An enum value's number changed

An enum value kept its name but has a new number. Binary data carries the number, so old data now decodes to a different value or an unknown one.

Enum numbers are permanent: add a new value instead.

## FL1030

**enum-value-renamed** — An enum value was renamed

An enum number is now spelled differently. Binary data is unaffected, but generated code and JSON encodings that use value names break.

## FL1031

**encoding-changed** — A number's wire encoding changed

The encoding of a number changed between incompatible representations, for example Protobuf `int32` to `sint32` (zigzag) or `fixed64` to `uint64` (varint). The binary data of one is misread by the other even when the values would fit.

Keep the encoding; changes between `int32`, `uint32`, `int64`, `uint64` and `bool` are compatible on the wire, as are `sint32`/`sint64`, `fixed32`/`sfixed32` and `fixed64`/`sfixed64`, subject to the value ranges, which Faultline checks separately.

## FL1032

**number-not-reserved** — A removed field's number was not reserved

A field or enum value was removed and its number was not added to `reserved`. Nothing breaks yet, but a later change can reuse the number for something else, and data written by older versions will then be misread as the new field.

Add `reserved <number>;` (and the name) when removing a field or value.

## FL1033

**reserved-number-reused** — A reserved number was reused

A new field or enum value uses a number or name that an older version reserved. Data written with the retired meaning still exists and will be misread.

Pick a number that was never used.

## FL1034

**reservation-removed** — A reservation was removed

Numbers or a name are no longer `reserved`, which allows them to be reused by accident.

## FL2001

**operation-removed** — An operation was removed

An operation (an HTTP method and path, or an RPC method) no longer exists. Clients calling it receive errors.

Deprecate the operation first and remove it in a major version.

## FL2002

**operation-added** — An operation was added

A new operation (an HTTP endpoint or an RPC method) was added.

## FL2003

**operation-id-changed** — An operationId changed

The `operationId` changed. The wire contract is unaffected, but generated SDKs usually derive method names from it, so client code stops compiling.

## FL2004

**operation-moved** — An operation moved

An operation is served under a new path or name, with everything else unchanged. Clients calling the old path or name receive errors, but only the address changed: updating it is the whole migration.

Keep the old path or name working, for example as a deprecated alias, until clients have moved.

## FL2010

**parameter-added** — A parameter was added

An operation gained a parameter. A new *required* parameter breaks every existing client.

## FL2011

**parameter-removed** — A parameter was removed

An operation no longer declares a parameter. Clients still sending it may be rejected or silently ignored.

## FL2012

**parameter-requirement-changed** — A parameter became required or optional

Making a parameter required breaks clients that omit it.

## FL2013

**parameter-serialization-changed** — Parameter serialization changed

The `style`, `explode`, `allowReserved` or `allowEmptyValue` of a parameter changed, so the same value is written differently on the wire (for example `tags=a,b` instead of `tags=a&tags=b`).

## FL2020

**request-body-added** — A request body was added

An operation now accepts a request body. A *required* body breaks clients that send none.

## FL2021

**request-body-removed** — A request body was removed

An operation no longer accepts a request body. Clients sending one may be rejected.

## FL2022

**request-body-requirement-changed** — A request body became required or optional

Making the request body required breaks clients that send none.

## FL2030

**media-type-added** — A media type was added

A request or response gained a media type. Additional request media types are safe; additional response media types only matter to clients that do not send `Accept`.

## FL2031

**media-type-removed** — A media type was removed

A request or response no longer supports a media type. Clients sending it (requests) or asking for it (responses) fail.

## FL2040

**response-added** — A response status was added

An operation documents a new response status. Clients with exhaustive status handling may not expect it.

## FL2041

**response-removed** — A response status was removed

An operation no longer documents a response status. Clients are not affected by responses they no longer receive, but the change may reflect changed behaviour.

## FL2050

**response-header-added** — A response header was added

A response gained a header.

## FL2051

**response-header-removed** — A response header was removed

A response no longer includes a header. Clients reading it lose information.

## FL2052

**response-header-requirement-changed** — A response header became required or optional

A header that was always sent may now be missing.

## FL2060

**security-requirement-added** — A security alternative was added

An operation accepts an additional combination of credentials. Existing clients are unaffected.

## FL2061

**security-requirement-removed** — A security alternative was removed

An operation no longer accepts a combination of credentials. When the removed combination is anonymous access, the operation now requires authentication.

## FL2070

**callback-added** — A callback was added

An operation now makes callback requests to the client.

## FL2071

**callback-removed** — A callback was removed

An operation no longer makes a callback; clients waiting for it are affected.

## FL2072

**webhook-added** — A webhook was added

The API sends a new webhook.

## FL2073

**webhook-removed** — A webhook was removed

The API no longer sends a webhook; receivers depending on it are affected.

## FL2080

**message-added** — A message type was added

An operation carries a new kind of message. Applications that receive it accept more; consumers of an application that sends it may not recognize it.

## FL2081

**message-removed** — A message type was removed

An operation no longer carries a kind of message. Producers still sending it to an application that received it are refused; consumers of an application that sent it stop getting it.

## FL3001

**streaming-changed** — An RPC changed between unary and streaming

A request or response of a remote procedure became a stream of messages, or stopped being one. Clients and servers disagree on the call's shape, and every call fails.

Add a new method with the new shape and deprecate the old one.
